speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Speaker, Sir, first, let me thank the Leader and Members of this House for allowing me to make this Statement on National Service (NS) training deaths in the midst of the debate on the President's Address.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I have requested to do so to address the concerns of Members here and the public over this matter.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I think we are right to be concerned as every NS death should be treated with utmost seriousness, whether it is in Parliament, the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) or the Home Team.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Any death among SAF soldiers or Home Team personnel is grievous.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These are our security forces who serve this nation with loyalty, commitment and pride.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They keep us safe, they defend our island home, often in challenging and dangerous circumstances knowing the risks to themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We know that no words can replace their loss.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We grieve together with them even as we honour the memory of their precious sons who served and sacrificed for our country.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF and Home Team will continue to assist their families as best as we can.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And I believe it can be done, even as National Servicemen train realistically and effectively to protect us and defend Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But achieving zero fatalities can only be achieved with constant vigilance, no lesser.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because on any given day, thousands of National Servicemen run around in challenging conditions, they move vehicles on air, land and sea, in Singapore and overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the SAF, modern military platforms travel at high speeds and our exercise tempos are very quick.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: All of us recognise the higher risks in military training because even for mass civilian activities, whether it is marathons, swims or cycling events, fatalities occur.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We read about them and they occur for a variety of innocent reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we must design our safety systems and enforce them so that training deaths within the SAF can be eliminated.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a difficult goal to achieve, to get it right every time, whenever a platoon or company that goes out on exercise, whether it is day or night.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But we must constantly improve the rigour of our safety systems to reach that goal because, if we do not, it may mean another precious son lost to a family.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Members in the House – Mr Dennis Tan1, Mr Henry Kwek2, Mr Vikram Nair3 and Mr Ganesh Rajaram4 – have filed questions on two recent NS deaths within the SAF and on general matters related to training safety.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I propose to address their queries in this Statement.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Here, I want to beg the House's indulgence and patience.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will give details as much as we know.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Both were serving their full-time NS: 3SG Chan had served for one year and eight months; CFC Lee for four months.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We treat each training related death with utmost seriousness.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We deal with it at the highest level within the SAF and MINDEF.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Armed Forces Council (AFC) convenes an independent Committee of Inquiry (COI) to examine thoroughly the circumstances leading to the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It is a four-member team chaired by a senior civil servant from outside MINDEF and includes a senior doctor from the public sector.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It can access all relevant information, access any personnel, haul them up to investigate the circumstances leading to death and they will determine events or persons that contributed to the event, to the death and make recommendations to rectify any lapses found.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Separately from the SAF and MINDEF, the Police conducts parallel investigations and the Coroner may decide to hold a public inquiry.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The police conducted an investigation into the circumstances of the incident.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The police found no defect with the infantry fighting vehicle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The police found from scene evidence and witness information, that its path forward was halted due to an obstruction.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sergeant Chan, who was commander of the vehicle, gave orders for the driver to reverse slowly down the hill.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The commander who was stationed in the turret, with his upper body clear of the vehicle structure, was giving instructions to the driver directing him to reverse and where to reverse.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All confirmed that the driver was continuing to reverse slowly, and in accordance with the commander’s instructions, when the vehicle traversed over a flat granite rock for about 4 metres before the vehicle became stuck on a large boulder, holding up the vehicle undercarriage.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The commander instructed the driver to turn the steering wheel in an attempt to gain traction when suddenly the vehicle dropped down over the rock rolling sideways before coming to rest further down the slope.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sergeant Chan was ejected from the vehicle and suffered significant injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Life support was commenced at the scene before he was airlifted to hospital where he was later pronounced deceased.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The police investigation established that there was no defect with the vehicle, and there was no suggestion that the driver was doing anything other than reversing very slowly, and at the specific direction of Sergeant Chan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The police considered it was a very unfortunate incident whilst deployed in difficult terrain in ‘black out’ conditions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was noted by the police that the driver was driving in compliance with SAF policy at the time of the incident, and under the specific instruction from Sergeant Chan.” These are the findings of the Queensland authorities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI further determined that Sergeant Chan and his platoon mates were sufficiently trained and qualified to participate in the exercise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They had no mental and physical conditions that could have affected their fitness to participate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The medical and safety coverage provided was found to be timely, adequate and proper.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, the COI conducted interviews with SAF soldiers at the exercise to piece together the chronology of events that led to the Bionix overturning.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The mishap occurred during night training for Bionix units.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For Members' information, Armour units do this regularly, because they have to become proficient to fight at night or under conditions of poor visibility.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is something that they must learn to do.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They have issued a night vision device which allows them to see in darkness, but it was not working.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is needed if armoured vehicles are to move at night.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Without the night vision device, armoured vehicles can move but only with the driver's hatch open and headlights switched on for better visibility.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: However, according to the driver, Sergeant Chan felt that the headlights “would give away their position to the enemy” and decided to continue training without headlights.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Accounts from his platoon mates to the COI attest to Sergeant Chan's strong motivation and high standards of performance during training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sergeant Chan was zealous in his training and probably wanted to complete the night mission assigned to their armour unit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Unfortunately, in the darkness, the vehicle entered an area with a steep incline and boulders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At that point, Sergeant Chan stopped the vehicle, dismounted to assess the surroundings and found that a boulder was blocking the vehicle.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He re-mounted the Bionix, sitting on the top edge of the vehicle commander hatch and told the driver to open his hatch and switch on the vehicle’s headlights so that they could reverse away from this area.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Unfortunately, as they were doing so, the vehicle overturned on the steep embankment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The three other soldiers in that Bionix did not suffer any injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI concluded that Sergeant Chan’s injuries resulted from him being thrown out of the vehicle as it overturned, causing his demise.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Queensland coroners’ report agreed that this was the cause of this event.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The report said, “…in the circumstances I find that Sergeant Chan died when he was ejected from the vehicle which he was directing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is unfortunate that he took the decision to position himself with a significant portion of his body outside the vehicle.” The coroner's report continues, “…the incident is none other than a very unfortunate accident due to the nature of the difficult terrain and the operation then being performed.” Arising from their investigations, the Queensland police found no basis to charge any person.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If he cannot do this, because you are much better protected inside the vehicle than out, the vehicle must stop.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI also recommended stronger compliance and checks on night vision devices (NVDs) and to enforce the wearing seatbelt rule for passengers when the vehicle is moving.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF has followed up and also implemented additional training for armoured vehicle commanders on uneven terrain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF has also implemented drills for day-to-night and night-to-day transitions and this includes NVDs and other night fighting equipment on the checklist which need to be in working order.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Wearing seatbelts is enforced, with disciplinary actions taken against those who have not done so.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sergeant Chan’s death was classified as a training-related incident and compensation offered to the family.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Sergeant Chan’s parents accepted the honours of a military funeral.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Armour formation paid their last respects to a dedicated commander whom they are proud to call one of their own.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To investigate Corporal Lee's death, all the processes that I have described for Sergeant Chan, the COI, police investigations and Coroner's inquiry are yet to be completed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I will only share information from our own internal investigations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When Members have clarifications later – and I encourage you to ask for clarifications – I will share what we have, with some caveats, that the COI and the independent Coroner's inquiry, if held, and the Police investigations will have to come to their own facts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: An SAF medic attended to Corporal Lee to bring down his core temperature and he was evacuated to the camp's Medical Centre where body-cooling measures and treatment were instituted by the SAF medical team there.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He was taken to Changi General Hospital (CGH) and warded in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Following the incident, the Army declared a safety timeout for all training and also specifically reviewed training that posed risks of heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During the timeout, commanders were reminded of the importance of safety measures which include hydration regimes, temperature-taking regimes, management of the work-rest cycle – I will explain what this means – and identification of personnel who could be at greater risk of heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These are currently in place; these are preventive safety measures against heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are a tropical island, hot and humid.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2010, the SAF convened a workgroup, which included many external experts, to address this specific problem.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This workgroup recommended clinical practice guidelines that were endorsed by MOM and the then-Singapore Sports Council.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, we take the recorded ambient temperature.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If it exceeds a certain level during training, rest periods are mandated at appropriate intervals to allow soldiers to cool down.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is one of the recommendations of the expert panel which the SAF follows dutifully.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And it is not just taking a thermometer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We use a wet-bulb globe temperature heat stress monitor.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is a hand-held device which will give you the ambient temperature, calculated with the humidity.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And based on that, the SAF institutes work-rest cycles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If it is below a certain temperature, for instance, you can exercise for 30 minutes, but you must rest for 15 minutes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Above 33oC, you must exercise for 15 minutes and rest for 30 minutes and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Commanders and soldiers are reminded to look out for signs and symptoms of heat injury during training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the event of heat injury, we have on-site cooling measures which include the removal of clothes and application of ice or water to the affected serviceman.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF medical centres have customised-built evaporative body-cooling units for heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As these two cases show, after every training-related death, independent and impartial investigative processes will determine the key facts, arrive at appropriate conclusions and we will take corrective measures to prevent mistakes from being repeated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This includes punishing those who contributed to the death through reckless and negligent acts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF servicemen can be charged and punished in the civilian criminal Courts, even if their acts were committed within the SAF, as part of their duty.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have said so in this House previously but these examples bear repeating for their salutary warnings.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2012, an SAF vehicle overturned during an exercise and it caused the death of a soldier.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The officer was found to have committed a rash act and attempted to pervert the course of justice.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In all cases, prosecutions of SAF servicemen in criminal Courts are based on independent Police investigations and when the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) decides that there are sufficient grounds to prosecute.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be the criminal Courts that determine the level of culpability and commensurate punishments.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Separately, the Coroner may hold an inquiry to determine the causes of death and contributory factors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF fully accepts these judicial processes and, indeed, deems them necessary to achieve and maintain a zero-fatality training safety system.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know that there are accusations against the commanders of Corporal Lee, but we should let the independent COI and Police investigations fully investigate the circumstances to establish the facts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Those that deserved to be punished will be punished.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If any persons are found to have been negligent or culpable, they will be punished according to the law, both in civilian and military Courts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we must be careful not to discourage or unfairly punish commanders who are executing their responsibilities dutifully, because many commanders are National Servicemen, too, who take seriously this mission we in society have imposed on them – to train capable fighting units able to defend Singapore against all threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And he is serious about his duty and he wants to build a fighting unit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We must be careful that we do not discourage them or punish them unfairly.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Indeed, we have many positive examples of commanders who risk their own safety to protect trainees.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In 2013, NSF commander Lieutenant Kamalasivam pulled a recruit down to take cover in the grenade-throwing bay.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He held the grenade, took out the safety pin and released the grenade lever.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Lieutenant Kamalasivam's first instinct was to pull the recruit down and cover himself over him.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Thankfully, both suffered minor injuries which they recovered from.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even if there was no ill-intent, are NSF commanders trained adequately and do they have the maturity to exercise good judgement and consciousness regarding training safety?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is what Nominated Member Ganesh Rajaram asked.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: All commanders undergo safety training both in the Specialist Cadet School (SCS) and Officer Cadet School (OCS).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In addition, we have Unit Safety Officers and these are ex-regulars who have held senior appointments, who support the safe conduct of exercises.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These Unit Safety Officers do not just have book learning; they have actual experience conducting and taking part in training and operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But Unit Safety Officers cannot be everywhere all the time.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, for instance, for Exercise Wallaby, we sent 4,000 to 5,000 men down to Shoalwater Bay to train.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A strong safety culture and a zero-fatality training system can only be achieved if every soldier has that ingrained concern for the well-being of himself and his peers.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: On the ground, it is the creed of the commanders to take care of their men.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If you do not know how to take care of your men and if it is shown that you do not know how to take care of the men, we will remove your command position, we will remove your rank.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Commanders are taught to encourage their men and buddies to flag out when they do not feel well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Individual soldiers are advised to highlight risky behaviour and safety breaches and they can report them to their superiors without fear of reprisal.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is a 24-hour training safety hotline for commanders and soldiers to report safety incidents and near-misses.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, not only when something happens, but a near-miss, report it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have another External Review Panel on SAF Safety (ERPSS).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It consists of prominent safety experts and professionals outside the SAF and it helps MINDEF scrutinise our safety management system.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have attached a list of its members.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The current Chairman is Mr Heng Chiang Ngee, who was also Chairman of the Workplace Safety and Health Council till March this year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This panel reports to the Minister on the rigour of the system and presents recommendations to improve.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: With these multiple layers of safety and with experts within and outside assisting the SAF, we can move decisively to make zero training deaths the norm.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I know it is difficult but it must be done.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this shows that zero fatalities can be achieved with effort.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Chief of Defence Force and the Service Chiefs have assured me that safety has always been and will continue to get their highest command attention to achieve zero fatalities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we need every level to play their part, down to the individual commander and soldier, to protect their own well-being and that of their men and their buddies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our SAF commanders know that precious sons are entrusted to us when they train during NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will work in unison and instil in every commander and soldier a strong sense of responsibility in ensuring training safety at all levels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I would encourage Members in this House to seek any clarification because Parliament is a critical and appropriate forum to ensure that we have done all that is possible to make safety a top priority so that every soldier is well-protected as they defend Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This morning, I received an email from a concerned mother who has a son in National Service now.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: She says that she understood from her son that the "tekan" culture still exists in National Service.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister, first, is this "tekan" culture allowed; second, where is the channel for reporting such cases; and, third, what would be the range of punishments for the officers involved.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will be the same answer as she would give.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The excuses may mean very little because the TSRs are there to protect your men.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My follow-up question is in relation to the unfortunate death of SCDF CPL Kok at Tuas View Fire Station.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can the Minister for Home Affairs assure us that all steps are being taken to help ensure that such an unfortunate and unnecessary death does not happen again?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think we fully recognise that there is a need to fully discuss the unfortunate and tragic SCDF incident and Members should file Parliamentary Questions and they should be aired in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: However, I am prepared to permit this question if the Minister for Home Affairs wishes to respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their grief, their loss at CPL Kok’s passing, a young life which has been prematurely cut short.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The family is at the front and centre of our thoughts and prayers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, as we talk about the other matters, I want to emphasise that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is tragic that this has happened, and we must, and will, do right by them and by the late CPL Kok.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will now also deal with two other points, that is, what happened in this case and, third, what we can do to try and make sure that this does not happen again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will release the details that we can at this stage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a fair bit of evidence as to what happened, both witnesses' and objective evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is not appropriate for me to go into the details, the facts, at this stage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be a Board of Inquiry (BOI).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The majority of the members will be from outside the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will almost certainly also be criminal proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Attorney-General's Chamber has told me that, after reviewing the facts at this stage.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on the facts that I have seen, I think so, too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am usually very careful about saying these things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the BOI will look into the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The facts will also come out in public, through Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What I can say is that the conduct was unacceptable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a clear and serious violation of the rules and there can be no excuse for the conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They make people like CPL Kok do dangerous things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And people who do this do not think.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They do not think how it can go wrong and, when it does go wrong, a life is lost, needlessly lost.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is imperative that we see what went wrong and learn the lessons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What more can we do to stop this sort of behaviour?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Commanders emphasise that to the officers and all new enlistees are told about the rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Detentions have been given when infractions have been found.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do we make sure that there is zero tolerance?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once they are finalised, I will announce them next week.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Meanwhile, I have made it clear that, hereafter, it will be a command responsibility to ensure that such conduct is not repeated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And hereafter, Unit Commanders will be held responsible for anything like this that happens, any kind of conduct that is in violation or in breach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Commissioner Erip Yap has sent a letter in very clear terms on this yesterday to all officers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has also personally spoken to the Commanders, emphasising that message, and the same will be done with the other Home Team agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there will be zero tolerance and we will have to do, we will do our best not to let this happen again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have a few questions for the Minister for Defence pertaining to his earlier Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My first question pertains to the COI concerning 3SG Gavin Chan and the finding that his night vision device was not working.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Does the COI report indicate whether the non-serviceability of the night vision device could have been a critical factor in the incident, in that, 3SG Chan, had his device been working properly, could have taken some remedial action before the obstacle was discovered along the path where the vehicle was moving?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question is related to that, whether, in future, MINDEF would consider making public COI reports as a form of closure for the public, with, of course, the relevant details redacted?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These could include sensitive information on behalf of the family and other operational reasons to redact certain information.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Speaker, I thank the Member for his questions.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I mentioned that we have now, henceforth, decided that we want to give as much information as we can and, as Mr Pritam Singh says, apart from sensitive issues or security reasons.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For Singaporeans who have served NS, they will not be unfamiliar with this word, "keng".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, the commanders will use it, with the good intention, to make the soldier work harder to give their best and also for the unit camaraderie.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, they say “do not keng" or “do not skive”.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we do know that, sometimes, soldiers are genuinely unwell and are, hence, not able to perform up to mark.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes the commanders are not able to read this right, or make a right judgement and, sometimes, not give the soldiers the benefit of the doubt and, therefore, to take him off from the training.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I want to ask the Minister, how does the SAF strike a balance, especially, in our case, where some of our National Servicemen are just fresh from school and may not have the temperament and ability to make the right decision to manage such situations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, how do we use more positive ways to encourage our soldiers to give of their best rather than a negative way of saying "don't keng" and, therefore, that is how we should go about?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Should we look at how we can eradicate this form of practice that we see even in the good old days?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Till today, I believe this is still happening.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we use a more positive way to encourage soldiers to give of their best?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If he feels unwell, he can flag himself out.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whether you think he is not completely truthful is beside the point.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He has the prerogative to flag himself out.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can train him to do the same exercise later, slowly, gradually, but that is a command decision.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But as these two examples show, that is not really the culture that prevails.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our young men who do NS are highly motivated, in the case of Gavin Chan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: He wanted to complete the exercise for his unit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the case of Dave Lee, he completed the eight-kilometre fast march.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I am not sure that it is accurate to characterise this dilemma between pushing people because they are inherently not as motivated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Our experience is that National Servicemen are motivated and, if they are not, then it is part of your skillsets to motivate him, to give him confidence, to be able to complete the exercise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this shows the seriousness of the matter that the Ministers themselves take every death seriously.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a serviceman myself, I think tough training is absolutely important.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the things that I think was a little bit troubling and which came out in social media as well, both in relation to CFC Dave Lee as well as to CPL Kok was the allegation of abuse, abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think both Ministers are clear that this should not happen.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My suggestion would be that National Servicemen be given an opportunity, perhaps a whistleblower's channel, somewhere outside the respective units perhaps directly to the Ministry, in the event there is such abuse or fear of such abuse, especially if the fear is that the unit's culture encourages that, in which case they would be afraid of reporting within the unit.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When death occurs, emotions are riled up, you have many views, some substantiated, some are unsubstantiated, which is why I said that, this House, Members here also play a critical role in making sure that safety gets top priority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As we have shown in the case of 3SG Gavin Chan, the COI established fully the facts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If there were people culpable, as previous COIs have shown, they were held responsible.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, in any case, in any death where people are culpable or negligent, they will be dealt with according to criminal law or in our military Courts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think we have enough cases to show that all of us want to have a zero-fatality system.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If Members have any other suggestions, I am happy to hear them and see whether we can incorporate them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But I want to assure you, this gets top-most priority, gets top attention at MINDEF and the SAF.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And especially important because I think in this kind of situation, particularly when there is tough training, the psychological state would actually affect the physical performance.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It can be not just on an individual level but affecting an entire section, platoon.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Under this kind of situation, a soldier may just push himself to the extreme.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope that maybe we can also look at, in the future, how do we have more psychological support in the army, in the training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI's primary mission is to establish the facts that led to the incident and cause of death, the contributory factors.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is quite clear and I think we understand that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If the psychological preparation of soldiers was inadequate, it will be flagged out.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And, yes, we pay attention to the psychology of the men.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is part and parcel of our military training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think I understand what the Member wants, but we have to understand that the COI's job is to determine the facts and, in the process, usually, they interview many soldiers who give different accounts.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First of all, it may be emotionally trying for the parents to sit there and to hear many accounts of the same thing happening again and again and, even as I recount it, 3SG Chan's events, it is very difficult.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is why we asked them for permission, can we reproduce this coroner's report?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Most of our SAF commanders are National Servicemen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To points that, with this culture, there might be abuse, yes, I believe that some of it may have gone overboard.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But by and large, our National Servicemen, our NS commanders, are decent, young men, who are doing their duty that we asked them to do to raise fighting units.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We want to strike a balance, we have to make sure that we, in this House, send the appropriate signal; we, in leadership, send the appropriate signal.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But if you do your job dutifully, all the facts will come out and you need not fear, but continue to do your job.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: What is this protocol and is it sufficient to prevent heatstroke?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I would also want to ask whether the thermometer that CFC Dave Lee was using was in good order.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, these are the facts that the COI and the Police must investigate.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, any findings that I give, I will put the caveat that these are internal investigations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whether the thermometer was working, I think we have to investigate that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not know, I presume it was because it would be used for others as well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Hydration protocols, yes, we do, and there are certain volumes that one has to take in.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think those with sons in NS will recognise that it is done de rigueur.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Everybody stands up with their water bottle and takes the requisite volume and you have to prove that you have drunk it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because some worry that some people may feel that they have enough water and they pour it on the ground.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And all these measures, for good units, they recognise that it is done, strictly followed because it is meant to protect our soldiers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I share his sentiment and I feel for the families for their loss.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, the Minister has answered most of my questions.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I just want to elaborate on one point about empathy and the maturity of commanders.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I have got a son who is entering National Service next year.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When I look at myself compared to him when I did my National Service, I would like to think I was a lot more matured than him going in.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I think that is because, as the society matures, kids are taken a lot better care of and they are more pampered at home.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have got kids who are going into NS who are not of the same build of before and I would like to think they are not as hardy.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Having said that, in terms of commanders, whether they are section commanders or officers of other rank, does the army focus on qualities like empathy as well as being able to assess how a kid is doing vis-a-vis performance?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Because, to be fair, I do not think it is intentional, I think all commanders and all National Servicemen want to perform at the best of their ability.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But, sometimes, it is difficult to tell and maybe they would need a lot more training in this area.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, if the Minister could share if there is such training and if it is going to be enhanced, given that we are getting generations coming in that may be a little less hardy than what we were, growing up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I can summarise the Member's question: how do we select commanders to have the necessary maturity and wherewithal to make good judgements?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this debate and in the President's Address, think of what Singapore is doing with NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Very few countries have been able to maintain NS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are taking every 18-year-old, 19-year-old for two years, put them together and, say as part of nation-building, as part of building up a defence force or a good Home Team, mix together, lead one another, train, work together, fight together.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Do that in any society, you get the full plethora of the frailties of human nature.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And even for that kind of activity, there were reported deaths for a variety of reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Can we step up the activities so that they can make good judgements?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You know that in Officer Cadet School (OCS), we have situational tests.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We put people together, give them situations and assess how they respond.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, yes, that is incorporated in trying to figure out the psychology elements that make a good leader and to see whether this chap has it or not.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have succeeded in our NS and this is why it is so important that we give it top-most priority when it comes to safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You give them to us, to the Police, to the SCDF for two years; we want to train them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We want to return them to you well-trained and safe.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have two supplementary questions but not relating to 3SG Gavin.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, in respect of the answer that the Minister has just given to a previous question, the Minister mentioned about empathy training, possibly during Command School at OCS or SISPEC.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The basis for my question is that I think those of us who have done National Service will also realise that, for some commanders, you may not see this in OCS or in SISPEC, but after they have gotten the rank, somehow the rank got to them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that is where the abuse of power, the tendency for abuse may happen.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Perhaps in very small numbers, but, nonetheless, this is something that the Minister may wish to consider looking into.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question relates to the Minister's information just now where you mentioned that the second review panel will be – correct me if I have heard you wrongly – given access to the COI reports.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Minister also consider that on other training safety-related reports, perhaps of lesser importance, let us say an intra-SAF Board of Inquiry (BOI) report relating to some accidents or incidents which may not even involve any actual casualty but, nonetheless, relating to training safety, would this panel be given access to such reports so that they have a good overview of the kind of incidents that may happen in the SAF and to be able to provide suggestions for improvement?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Speaker, on the Member's first question in terms of post-commission training for those who might be susceptible to abuse their position of authority, as I have said, if you are in that position, the safety counts first.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have the TSRs there so that, regardless of your empathy level, or your authoritativeness, you follow them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We can consider training them, but remember that these sons are given to us for two years, to the extent possible, all of them are given safety training while they are in Specialist Cadet School or OCS.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: My own position is that there will be certain security elements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Whether we want to include them to assess serious injuries, I think the Member's point was not deaths, or COIs or BOIs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Certainly, if the ERPSS feels that they can do more work, I will be happy to ask them if they could also be included.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Minister will agree that the thicker you make the TSRs, the more difficult it could actually be for the commanders in the field.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister referred earlier to the fact that commanders actually need certain skills.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is there an on-going system to assess whether there are deficits in the attitudes, as well as the skills of commanders in the field?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Is there an on-going system to ensure that, if such deficits are discovered, they can be remedied?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We receive, for two years the entire spectrum of abilities from society for males; all of them come to us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have fairly rigorous selection criteria for commanders – OCS, Specialist Cadet School.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Are there some that you chose as commanders that are not fit to be?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If there are attributes which show up and you do something wrong, they will be called out because safety is not negotiable, as we tell them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, it is a difficult question that you have asked: do we constantly second-guess and check on them?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In honesty, it is difficult, but remember, in the military, there is a hierarchical situation, so I take it that the commanders above them would spot it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There are these annual reviews, but let me try to simplify this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We take it that commanders have various skill sets and various empathy levels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But let this message be very clear: when it comes to safety, it gets top-most priority.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When it comes to the welfare of your men, that is your top-most priority, whatever your skill sets, whatever your empathy level.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You protect the well-being of your men first.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have a family member who is serving in the same platoon as CFC Dave Lee.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And following the incident, there were many parents and National Servicemen in the same platoon who were sharing concerns and worries.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister if the Ministry is familiar with the state of affairs of the motivation and the level of our National Servicemen in the same platoon being in so close contact with the deceased.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As well as whether has conversation been taking place with the family members to assure them that the safety protocols are in place and their sons can continue to be in the exercise and various operational readiness that they are being put through in the camp?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We checked all processes, even when it is not related to heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Then, specifically, for heat injuries, make sure that the protocols are in place and then we restart the training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I was watching whether the social media furore over this would divide, as the Member rightly alluded to, the men and the commanders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we have to learn from these lessons that when something wrong happens, does it divide or does it unite?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It does not only apply to the SAF, it applies to other problems in society.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think in this quiet Chamber where we have the equanimity to examine all the facts, to ask why our men are doing this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Are there a majority who are just trying to do their duty?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We then come to the very decisions on what we need to do to strengthen the system; but never degrade it, never reduce the trust, but build up this cache.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And each year that we can do this, the SAF will get stronger, the SAF will get safer to protect us.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We will take one more question, Mr Yee Chia Hsing.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, after every incident that happened, the danger is that when this current batch of servicemen graduate, move on or retire, the new batch of servicemen, all that they have are the TSRs that have been modified or added, but they are in a vacuum without context.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I am not sure whether we can change our safety training, also to put context to the TSRs when we do the training to say, “We put in this TSR because that incident happened and we lost a serviceman.” So that people would realise the importance of the TSRs for subsequent batches of servicemen.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Speaker, the Member has made a very essential point for safety management systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I used to be Minister for Manpower and he is absolutely right.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We went to countries that have very good safety systems.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Scandinavians have excellent safety systems because that is their culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we have to build a culture so that even when commanders change, even when National Servicemen change, we retain it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some of you may have worked in ExxonMobil where, before every meeting, they would give you a safety briefing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even if it is a 15-minute meeting, the organisers would give you a briefing to tell you where the exits are, to tell you what happens.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have to do that so that the safety systems are maintained and that is why we have Unit Safety Officers that build up this culture.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will take time, but we have gotten it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I believe if all of us give attention, as we did in 2012 to 2016, no fatalities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Let us go that extra mile and make sure that our sons remain safe.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Clerk will now proceed to read the Orders of the Day.
